score_basis: Non-statistical internal evidence-quality score based on current GOV.UK/Planning Inspectorate/Active Travel England and local-highway-authority guidance, with explicit London-borough jurisdiction handling and no inference of extinguished highway or PRoW rights from planning permission alone.

sources.label: GOV.UK stopping up orders
sources.fact: Updated 25 March 2025; section 247 removes highway rights to enable approved development and section 253 can start process while permission is in progress.

sources.label: GOV.UK apply to close or divert highway
sources.fact: The national online service covers sections 247/248/253 but explicitly is not for London boroughs; London jurisdiction must be handled through the relevant authority.

sources.label: GOV.UK stopping-up process guidance
sources.fact: Stopping up is the legal process for removing highway rights; planning permission alone does not remove those rights.

sources.label: Natural England PRoW landowner responsibilities
sources.fact: Definitive maps are legal records of public rights of way and landowners must not obstruct or endanger users.

sources.label: Natural England local highway authority responsibilities
sources.fact: Highway authorities must record, maintain and protect public rights of way; definitive map and statement is the legal network record.

sources.label: Planning Inspectorate rights-of-way guidance
sources.fact: Updated 22 April 2026; covers objections to definitive map and public path orders and remains procedural guidance rather than parcel-specific legal determination.

sources.label: Planning Inspectorate public path order procedures
sources.fact: Updated 22 April 2026; definitive map evidence is conclusive for recorded particulars at the relevant date but does not rule out higher rights.

sources.label: Planning Inspectorate PRoW and common land collection
sources.fact: Updated 21 January 2026 with 2026 public-rights/common-land forms and decisions; process status must be checked from the actual order/decision.

sources.label: Active Travel England public rights of way
sources.fact: PRoWs are highways; development should protect/enhance them and impacts may require planning agreements or conditions.

sources.label: Planning Inspectorate common-land works guidance
sources.fact: Updated 23 March 2026; certain works on regulated common land require separate consent and are not authorised by planning permission alone.

sources.label: Tower Hamlets stopping-up orders
sources.fact: London local-highway-authority guidance confirms highway rights are extinguished only when the legal stopping-up order is made; consultation/objection process applies.

sources.label: Cornwall public path orders
sources.fact: Official council guidance states planning permission does not itself allow closure, obstruction or diversion of a public right of way; the legal process must complete first.

examples.result: Planning permission is not treated as extinguishing highway or PRoW rights; an effective legal order is required.
The national DfT stopping-up online service is tagged NOT_FOR_LONDON_BOROUGHS; London authority process must be used for Barking & Dagenham context.
A definitive-map route intersecting a site is a legal-rights signal, not automatic development refusal; exact route and order status are required.
Absence from a simplified online map is not used as proof that no higher or unrecorded rights exist.
A public path may need diversion/extinguishment process even where the underlying development has planning permission.
Common-land works consent is kept separate from planning permission and highway/public-path processes.
Temporary construction closure or traffic order is not treated as permanent extinguishment of public rights.
No access/highway promotion occurs without exact parcel/site geometry, authoritative highway/PRoW record and completed legal-order evidence where required.
